briefing.headline: The simulation predicts that a five-day office mandate would roughly double attrition over the next 12 months, from about 631 to 1,377 leavers (746 more people, +115%), taking annual turnover from about 13% to about 28% of staff.
briefing.most_at_risk: Caregivers (+155%) and people with long commutes (+138%) react worst, especially parents of young children facing 85-to-90-minute commutes each way, who say they will start looking for hybrid jobs right away; managers (+140%) and mid-level staff (+134%) also show steep rises, and they are the hardest to replace.
risks: Departures would likely come quietly and in a wave: people say they will stay until they hold a hybrid offer, and competitors are actively hiring these skills, so the loss may show up suddenly rather than gradually.
Women (+127% vs +107% for men) and caregivers would leave at higher rates, which would weaken diversity and the leadership pipeline and could become a fairness and reputation issue.
Linking attendance to performance ratings is seen as a punishment, and top performers call it insulting; it would push out strong people and make ratings less about the quality of work.
design_changes: Remove attendance from performance ratings. Employees single it out as the most offensive part of the policy, and it adds nothing the attendance rule does not already achieve.
Move to three set office days instead of five, and let people work from home on days with late US or Europe client calls, so they do not face a long commute and an evening call on the same day.

Offer flexible start times to avoid peak traffic, plus a formal flexibility option for caregivers and long-distance commuters. Employees say the shuttle alone 'won't fix' a 90-minute commute, so do not rely on it.
briefing.confidence: medium, because every group and every sample voice points the same way (more leaving, with commute and caregiving as the main drivers), but this is a model built on only 48 voices, so treat the exact figure of 746 extra leavers as a rough indication of scale rather than a forecast.
